summary:
Visitors in Nord-Ovest stand under the national framework of Italy, which the parent record carries in full. The findings below are specific to this region: its own municipal measures, its own documented pattern of hate-motivated violence, and the custodial practice that would apply to a trans person detained here.

Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, allowing transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. LifeGate presents the measure as a milestone for transgender rights in the country, and ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs a parallel practice, Identita Alias, at municipality level and in its libraries.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city covering 2012 to 2025 shows that two of the constituent regions making up Nord-Ovest rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. That ranking is by raw counts of incidents and victims only; the source provides no per-capita or population denominator, so it establishes that violence is documented at scale here rather than that these regions are more dangerous per resident than smaller ones.

Custodial placement tracks legal sex. La Repubblica's 2013 investigation recorded a prison administration count of 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities: trans women were held in men's sections, prisoners who had undergone sex-change surgery were sent to the women's sections, and female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, count as men. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety. Protected sections, including the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples, imposed limitations that extended to partner visits.

The 2010 baseline for that practice was different in form and similar in effect: transgender prisoners were located in women's prisons, where they were often segregated for their own safety. In the 2011 Terni case, the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision.
tangentialFactors:
Italy announced plans in January 2010 for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison at Pozzale, near Florence, into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of the country's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, most convicted of drug or prostitution offences. Gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. La Repubblica reported in 2013 that the project was abandoned, and the same report states that the Pozzale scheme, which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano in Florence, was shelved.

The Milan registry is presented by its source as a national first, which sets a regional measure against a country-wide baseline in which no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination. Turin's Identita Alias practice runs alongside it at a lower administrative level, covering municipal services and libraries rather than a registry.

The regional ranking from Progetto Gionata rests on raw counts accumulated over thirteen years, so it tracks population size as well as incidence. It is evidence of a sustained documented pattern in these two constituent regions, not a per-capita comparison between them and the rest of Italy.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents of Milan can use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents through the registro di genere, the first such registry in Italy, established following a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Residents of Turin have access to the Identita Alias practice at the municipality and in city libraries.

For transgender prisoners, placement follows the sex recorded on the identity card rather than gender identity or surgical status. Hormone therapy has been refused on that basis, and isolation has been used when cells were unavailable, a practice the 2013 investigation described as the most inhumane means of preserving safety. Protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia and the section at Poggioreale restrict visits, including by partners.

The 2011 Terni ruling obliged the local health authority to fund a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity, with a July 2012 appellate decision following the appeal. Whether that reasoning has been applied in the prisons of this region is not documented in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Progetto Gionata's regional figures are raw counts of aggressions with no population denominator supplied, so the six-highest-victim ranking cannot be read as a per-capita risk comparison. That denominator remains unresolved in the sources.

The sources do not state whether Milan's gender registry affects state identity documents or passports, or whether it is confined to civic and municipal records. Turin's Identita Alias is described only at municipality and library level.

The current status of the Pozzale project after the 2013 report of its abandonment is unresolved; no later source confirms whether a dedicated facility for transgender prisoners exists anywhere in Italy.

No region-specific data was found on enforcement outcomes for hate-motivated violence against transgender people in Nord-Ovest, on prosecutions arising from the incidents counted by Progetto Gionata, or on whether the Terni hormone-therapy ruling has been applied in facilities holding prisoners from this region.
